extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners (patent agents/attorneys), patent law firm compliance officers, and participants in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures for USPTO disciplinary review of practitioner conduct, with particular focus on certifications of micro entity status, reasonable inquiry obligations, and applicable sanctions and mitigating factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification obligations under 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: A party presenting any paper to the USPTO certifies: (1) statements of the party's own knowledge are true; (2) statements on information and belief are believed to be true; and (3) statements are made with knowledge that knowingly and willfully falsifying, concealing, or making false statements is punishable under criminal statutes. Further, to the best of the party's knowledge, information and belief, formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances, the paper: (i) is not presented for an improper purpose (harass, delay, increase cost); (ii) contains legal contentions warranted by existing law or nonfrivolous argument for change; (iii) allegations and factual contentions have evidentiary support or are likely to after reasonable investigation; and (iv) denials of factual contentions are warranted on the evidence or reasonably based on lack of information or belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations may subject the presenter to penalties under 18 U.S.C. § 1001 and other statutes and may jeopardize the probative value of the paper. The certifying practitioner must form beliefs after a reasonable inquiry under the circumstances; mere reliance without inquiry may violate this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Micro entity eligibility requirements (37 C.F.R. § 1.29(a) / MPEP § 509.04(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify as a micro entity on a gross income basis the applicant must certify: (1) qualifies as a small entity without relying on government use license exception; (2) neither applicant nor inventor nor joint inventor has been named as inventor/joint inventor on more than four previously filed patent applications (with specified exceptions); (3) in the preceding calendar year, neither applicant nor inventor nor joint inventor had gross income exceeding three times the median household income as reported by the Census; and (4) neither applicant nor inventor nor joint inventor has assigned/granted/conveyed or is obligated to assign a license or other ownership interest to an entity that in the preceding calendar year had gross income exceeding three times the median household income.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certifications of micro entity status must be factually supported by the applicant's circumstances; practitioners presenting these certifications must ensure the underlying facts meet these criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful false claim of micro entity status may be fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: A willful false claim of micro entity status may be considered fraud on the USPTO and can adversely affect the proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities include 37 C.F.R. § 1.29(i), 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(1) and 18 U.S.C. § 1001. Practitioners should treat knowingly false certifications as potentially criminal and as grounds for adverse proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to conduct a reasonable inquiry before presenting certifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must form beliefs 'after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances' before presenting certifications (including micro entity certifications) to the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to conduct such inquiry (e.g., signing certifications based solely on representations from foreign associates without verification) can violate the Rules of Professional Conduct (37 C.F.R. § 11.18) and related duties of diligence and integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence obligation (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must act with reasonable diligence in representing a client. The Final Order found violation of § 11.103 by (i) not always conducting a reasonable inquiry under § 11.18 prior to presenting certifications of micro entity status, and (ii) failing to have adequate procedures to ensure certifications complied with USPTO regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining internal procedures, verification protocols, and timely responses to USPTO notices are part of meeting the diligence obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on conduct prejudicial to the integrity of the patent application process (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in conduct that is prejudicial to the integrity of the patent application process is prohibited. The practitioner was found to violate § 11.804(d) by failing to conduct reasonable inquiry and lacking adequate procedures to ensure compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions that undermine the integrity of the examination process (e.g., improper certifications) can trigger this violation; practitioners should ensure accuracy and process integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to correct entity status and pay deficient amounts per 37 C.F.R. § 1.28(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the USPTO issues a Notice of Payment Deficiency, entity status may be changed and deficient amounts paid in accordance with 37 C.F.R. § 1.28(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responding to Notices promptly and correcting filings/fees is required; failure to monitor or be aware of Notices can be problematic for practitioner diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner internal procedures and verification requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners and their firms should have procedures or guidelines to personally verify the underlying basis of Certifications of Micro Entity Status and to review, confirm, and audit submissions to the USPTO to ensure compliance with 37 C.F.R. § 11.18.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of appropriate measures include requiring further information/verification prior to submitting certifications, retroactively obtaining applicant certifications, and auditing assertions from foreign associates and applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors considered in imposing or tempering discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining discipline, the OED considered: (i) no prior professional discipline by USPTO; (ii) acknowledgment of lapses, contrition, and acceptance of responsibility; (iii) full cooperation with OED's investigation and provision of supplemental responses; (iv) sua sponte corrective action taken to comply with professional responsibilities; and (v) retroactive review and adoption of measures to prevent recurrence (including verifying assertions by foreign associates and applicants from China).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These mitigating factors may reduce the severity of sanctions; lack of such factors or aggravating conduct may increase discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible sanctions and related procedural outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreed-upon sanctions in this matter included a public reprimand, electronic publication of the Final Order in OED's FOIA Reading Room, and publication of a materially consistent notice in the Official Gazette. The practitioner also waived rights to reconsideration, review, or appeal, and each party bore their own costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary sanctions can include public reprimand, publication, and be used as aggravating factors in future proceedings; practitioners should expect publicity of disciplinary results and potential preclusion of appeals depending on agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO disciplinary jurisdiction authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director has jurisdiction over practitioner disciplinary matters pursuant to 35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D) and 32 and 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.19, 11.20, and 11.26.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes the procedural authority for OED investigations, settlements, and imposition/publication of discipline against registered practitioners.
